nameStory: The mica cap gets its sparkling name from the tiny, reflective cells that coat young mushroom caps like glittering mica flakes on a rock. These shimmery particles catch the light beautifully when you first spot them in the woods, though they often wear off as the mushroom ages. It's also called the 'glistening inky cap' because those same caps will eventually dissolve into black, ink-like liquid!
description: Mica caps are small, tawny-brown mushrooms that grow in impressive clusters around dead hardwood stumps and roots. Young caps sparkle with tiny reflective flakes and start oval-shaped before opening to bell or umbrella forms up to about 1¼ inches across. What makes them truly unique is their disappearing act - within hours of being picked, their gills slowly melt into black, inky liquid. These delicate fungi pack a lot of drama into their small stature, rarely exceeding 4 inches tall.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Small tawny-brown caps up to 1¼ inches across, covered in sparkly mica-like flakes when young that feel slightly gritty to touch. Look for fine grooves radiating from center to nearly the edge, like tiny wheel spokes.

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Gills start light colored but will slowly dissolve into black, drippy ink within hours of picking - a fascinating process called autodigestion that you can actually watch happen.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Slender whitish stems up to 4 inches tall that feel smooth and somewhat fragile. No ring around the stem, and stems often cluster tightly together at the base.

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Always grows in dense, crowded clusters that can contain dozens of individual mushrooms sprouting from the same base - never found growing alone.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Fresh specimens have a mild, earthy mushroom smell without any strong or unpleasant odors.

habitat: Look for mica caps clustered around rotting hardwood stumps, buried roots, and decaying wood debris in New England's deciduous and mixed forests. They're particularly fond of maple, oak, and birch wood, often appearing where old stumps are hidden under leaf litter. You'll find them from lowland woods to mid-elevation forests throughout the region.

seasonality.spring: Early clusters may appear on warm, wet days as temperatures rise, especially around stumps that stayed moist through snowmelt.
seasonality.summer: Peak season for mica caps, fruiting abundantly after summer rains. Look for fresh sparkly caps in the morning before the day's heat ages them.
seasonality.fall: Continues fruiting well into autumn, often producing some of the largest flushes as moisture returns and temperatures cool.
seasonality.winter: Rarely fruits during cold months, though you might spot old black remnants from fall fruiting still clinging to stumps.

funFact: Mica caps contain natural antibacterial compounds that scientists are studying for potential medical applications - so those little sparkly mushrooms might help develop future medicines!
confusionNotes: Nearly impossible to distinguish from Coprinellus truncorum without microscopic analysis - many 'mica cap' sightings may actually be this close relative. Both have the same sparkly caps and inky gill dissolution, grow in similar clusters, and inhabit the same types of dead wood.
contextualKnowledge: This mushroom was moved from the old genus Coprinus to Coprinellus in 2001 when DNA studies revealed that many 'inky cap' mushrooms weren't as closely related as previously thought. You might still see it listed as Coprinus micaceus in older field guides.
compareHints: Unlike the tiny Trooping Crumble Cap which grows in massive swarms of hundreds of mushrooms, mica caps form smaller but still impressive clusters. The related Firerug Inkcap tends to grow on burnt ground rather than rotting wood. Most other relatives in this genus lack the distinctive sparkly mica coating that makes this species so recognizable when fresh.
